title: What are memory-mapped files (`FileChannel.map` → `MappedByteBuffer`), how do they map a file region into memory for OS-paged, zero-copy access, and when are they useful (very large files, high-throughput I/O, inter-process shared memory)?
shortTitle: What are memory-mapped files, how do they work, and when are they useful?
keyPoints: FileChannel.map returns a MappedByteBuffer that maps a file region into the process virtual address space for direct read and write access.
The OS uses demand paging to load file pages only when first accessed, and writes dirty pages back lazily, giving zero-copy I/O with no per-access system call.
Three modes exist: READ_ONLY, READ_WRITE (shared, writes propagate to disk and other processes), and PRIVATE (copy-on-write, writes are local only).
MappedByteBuffer is limited to about two gigabytes per mapping because ByteBuffer indexes with int; the Foreign Memory API removes this ceiling.
Durability requires an explicit force() call because lazy write-back means data may be in memory only after a put.
There is no public unmap method on the old API; the mapping is released only when the buffer is garbage-collected, causing potential file-lock issues.
Use cases include very large files accessed randomly, high-throughput I/O (Kafka, Lucene), and inter-process shared memory without sockets.

s1_definition.oneliner: A memory-mapped file maps a file region into the process virtual address space via FileChannel.map, returning a MappedByteBuffer where the OS pages data on demand for zero-copy, high-throughput access.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Memory-mapped file** – a region of a file mapped directly into process memory so reading and writing the file becomes reading and writing memory, with no explicit read or write system calls.
- **`FileChannel.map(mode, position, size)`** – the Java API that creates the mapping and returns a `MappedByteBuffer`.
- **Demand paging** – the OS loads file pages into physical memory only when first accessed, and writes dirty pages back lazily.
- **Zero-copy** – no data is copied between a kernel buffer and a user buffer, because the application accesses the file pages directly.
- **Modes** – `READ_ONLY`, `READ_WRITE` (shared, writes go to disk), and `PRIVATE` (copy-on-write, writes stay local).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a giant archive book of every transaction, far too big to photocopy. Normal file reading is like asking a clerk to fetch and copy one page at a time. A memory-mapped file is like placing the entire archive on your desk, but each page appears only when you actually turn to it. You read and write pages directly, and the bank quietly syncs changes back to the master archive in the background.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  FileChannel.map(mode, position, size)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         MappedByteBuffer              │
  │   (virtual address space mapping)     │
  │                                       │
  │  get()/put() ──▶ memory access        │
  │       │                               │
  │       ▼                               │
  │  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐       │
  │  │  Page 0    │  │  Page 1    │ ...   │
  │  │  (loaded)  │  │ (not yet)  │       │
  │  └────────────┘  └────────────┘       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
       │                    ▲
       │  page fault        │  demand paging
       ▼                    │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         Operating System              │
  │   Page Cache ◀── File on Disk         │
  │                                       │
  │   Dirty pages ──▶ lazy write-back     │
  │   force()     ──▶ immediate flush     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```text
  Mapping Modes:

  READ_ONLY:    App ──read──▶ File pages (no writes)
  READ_WRITE:   App ◀──rw──▶ File pages ◀──▶ Other processes
  PRIVATE:      App ──cow──▶ Copy of pages (writes stay local)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A memory-mapped file maps a region of a file directly into the process virtual address space, so reading and writing the file becomes reading and writing memory. In Java you call `FileChannel.map` with a mode, a position, and a size, and you get back a `MappedByteBuffer`. The OS uses demand paging, loading file pages only when first accessed and writing dirty pages back lazily. This removes the per-access system call and the kernel-to-user copy, which is the zero-copy benefit.

The three modes serve different purposes. `READ_WRITE` lets writes propagate back to the file and to other processes, which is how inter-process shared memory works. `READ_ONLY` is safe for reporting. `PRIVATE` gives copy-on-write for what-if simulations without touching the original data.

In banking at National Bank of India, Pankaj designed an end-of-day ledger of fixed-size records stored as long values in paise. Reporting and settlement jobs read and updated balances by offset without loading the whole file. The critical rule is durability: because write-back is lazy, after writing a committed record you must call `force()` to flush to disk before reporting success, otherwise a crash could lose data that was only in memory.

The old API has two well-known problems. The two-gigabyte per-mapping limit comes from `ByteBuffer` indexing with `int`. And there is no public `unmap()` method, so the mapping stays alive until the garbage collector runs, which can lock files unexpectedly. The Foreign Function and Memory API solves both: `MemorySegment` supports the full `long` range, and closing the `Arena` unmaps immediately.

Remember one sentence: memory-mapped files give zero-copy, OS-paged access to file regions through `MappedByteBuffer`, but you must call `force()` for durability and use the Foreign Memory API for deterministic unmapping.
